readerTitle: The ad said five minutes. The sign-up took twenty-five.
caseNote: 가상 사례 (미용실 예약 앱 가입 과정, 신규 레스토랑 예약~첫 방문) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 가입 과정은 '가입 버튼'에서 끝나지 않는다. 광고의 약속에서 첫 성공 경험까지 하나의 여정으로 직접 걸어 보면, 고객이 떠나는 진실의 순간과 기대와 경험의 차이가 보인다.
misconception: 가입자가 이탈하면 가입 버튼이나 홈페이지를 고치면 된다. 가입만 받으면 일은 끝난 것이다.

sources.text: 고객 여정, 진실의 순간, 기대와 경험의 차이는 이 유닛의 개념 레슨(CUS-08-01, CUS-08-02, CUS-08-05)을 적용한 것
모든 수치와 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 가상 수치 계산 확인: 가입 양식 4분 + 인증 메일 대기 3분 + 서비스·영업시간 입력 10분 + 고객 명단 가져오기 8분 = 25분. 광고 약속 5분과의 차이 20분(5배).
레스토랑 사례의 '20분 대기'는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 실제 통계로 읽히지 않도록 카드에 illustrative 표시를 했습니다.

cards.title: The ad said five minutes. The sign-up took twenty-five.
body: Maya runs a small app that lets hair salons take bookings online. Her ad promises: "Start taking bookings in 5 minutes."
Plenty of salon owners sign up. Most never take a single booking. Her sign-up numbers look fine. Her business doesn't.

image.label: A stopwatch next to a phone showing a half-finished setup screen
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 미용실 카운터 위에 스마트폰, 화면에는 반쯤 채운 설정 화면. 옆의 초시계 바늘이 5분을 한참 넘어 25분을 가리킴. 실제 앱 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Where should Maya start?
body: She has a week and a small budget to fix the problem. What does she do first?

options.text: Redesign the home page to get even more sign-ups
options.feedback: More people would enter a path that already loses most of them. She'd pay for traffic and keep the same leak.

options.text: Sign up herself as a new salon, from the ad to the first real booking, and time each step
options.feedback: This maps the **customer journey**: every step a customer takes, not just the one you own. It's slow, but it shows where people actually stop.

options.text: Email a survey to owners who left
options.feedback: Useful later, but few will answer, and those who do may not remember the exact step that lost them.

cards.title: Maya's own sign-up, step by step.
body: The ad promised 5 minutes. A first booking took **25**. The longest stretch came after the sign-up was "done".

breakdown.label: Verify email
breakdown.detail: Waiting for the link to arrive

breakdown.label: Empty dashboard
breakdown.detail: Typing in services, prices and hours

breakdown.label: Import clients
breakdown.detail: Copying a contact list by hand

cards.title: The gap starts in the ad.
body: A salon owner opens the app between clients, expecting five minutes. At minute ten she is still typing prices into blank boxes. A customer walks in, and she closes the tab.
The steps aren't broken. Each one works. The problem is **expectations vs experience**: the ad set a promise the journey couldn't keep, so a normal setup felt like a failure.
Maya now has two levers: change the steps, or change the promise.

cards.title: Which step decides whether a salon stays?
body: Maya can only rebuild one step this month.

options.feedback: Cutting fields helps a little. But owners who get past it still hit the empty screen.
This is the **moment of truth**: when the owner sees the app do its job. Everything before it should rush people there.
By then the owner has decided. Fixing the exit saves few people who never saw the app work.

cards.title: Get to the first booking faster.
body: Maya cuts the form to email and salon name. New accounts open with common services and hours already filled in, ready to edit. A button sends a test booking to the owner's own phone in under a minute.
Then she rewrites the ad: "See your first booking in minutes. Add your full menu later." The promise now matches the path.

image.label: Journey line with the first booking moved close to the start
image.brief: 가로 여정 선 인포그래픽. 위쪽 '이전' 선은 길고 중간에 큰 빈 상자(Empty dashboard). 아래쪽 '이후' 선은 짧고, 시작 직후 휴대폰 알림 아이콘 "First booking"이 빛남. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Your own walk-through is biased.
body: Maya knows where every button is, so her map will look faster than reality. Watch two or three real new customers try it, without helping.
The journey also differs by customer. A one-chair salon and a ten-chair salon may stop at different steps.
And don't polish every step equally. Effort belongs near the moment of truth.

cards.title: Now it's a new restaurant.
body: Guests book online easily and get a text: "Your table is ready at 7:00." But reviews say the first visit felt cold. Many guests waited about 20 minutes at the door, with no one greeting them.
You can fix one thing first. Which?

options.feedback: It already works. You'd spend effort on the smooth part of the **journey** and leave the rough part alone.

options.text: Have a host greet every booked guest at the door and seat them on time, or say honestly how long
options.feedback: Arrival is the **moment of truth**, and the text set an **expectation** of a ready table. Meet it, or reset it kindly.

options.text: Send more reminder texts before the visit
options.feedback: Reminders help guests show up. They don't change what happens once guests are standing at the door.

cards.softwareNote: A welcome email that says "you're all set" works like that text. If the next screen is empty, the promise breaks right where trust is being decided.

cards.title: A sign-up ends at the first success, not the button.
body: Walk the whole path yourself, time it, and fix the step where customers decide.
**Try it today:** sign up for your own product or book your own service as a stranger. Write down every step until you get real value.
list: **Customer journey:** map every step, including ones you don't own
**Moment of truth:** find the step that decides who stays
**Expectations vs experience:** make your promise match the path
